definitions.definition: Basic beliefs that you accept as true without proof, which everything else is built on.
definitions.example: Like assuming the sun will rise tomorrow — you can't prove it, but you plan your day around it.

definitions.definition: The idea that every physical event has a physical cause, and nothing outside the physical world can affect it.
definitions.example: If you drop a glass, it breaks because of gravity and impact, not because a ghost pushed it.

definitions.definition: The belief that God exists completely on his own, needing nothing outside himself to exist or be who he is.
definitions.example: Unlike a plant that needs soil and water, God doesn't depend on anything else to exist.

definitions.definition: The idea that God has shown or told humans truths about himself that they couldn't figure out on their own.
definitions.example: Like a teacher giving you the answer key — you wouldn't know it without being told.

definitions.definition: Assumptions you take for granted before you start thinking or investigating something.
definitions.example: Before you play a board game, you assume the rules are fair — that's a presupposition.

definitions.definition: When a system of thought uses itself to prove itself, creating a loop that can't be escaped.
definitions.example: Using a dictionary to look up the meaning of the word 'dictionary' — it's circular.

definitions.definition: Reasoning from specific examples to a general rule, like assuming the sun will rise because it always has.
definitions.example: If you see ten white swans, you might think all swans are white — that's induction.

definitions.definition: The philosophical challenge that you can't logically prove that the future will be like the past.
definitions.example: Just because bread nourished you yesterday doesn't prove it will tomorrow — you assume it will.

definitions.definition: The idea that something proves itself to be true without needing outside evidence, especially the Bible's claim to be God's word.
definitions.example: Like the sun proving it's bright by shining — you don't need a flashlight to check.

definitions.definition: A basic statement accepted as true without proof, used as a starting point for reasoning.
definitions.example: In math, 'the whole is greater than the part' is an axiom — it's just assumed true.

definitions.definition: A belief about the nature of reality that you choose to hold, even if it can't be proven by science.
definitions.example: Believing that only physical things exist is a philosophical commitment, not a scientific fact.

definitions.definition: The assumption that the laws of nature are the same everywhere and at all times.
definitions.example: Believing that gravity works the same on Earth and on Mars is trusting the uniformity of nature.

definitions.definition: A logical mistake where you assume the thing you're trying to prove as part of your argument.
definitions.example: Saying 'the Bible is true because it's God's word' assumes God exists, which is what you're trying to prove.

definitions.definition: Mixing up two different types of things, like treating a method as if it were a conclusion.
definitions.example: Asking 'what color is the number seven?' is a category error — numbers don't have colors.

definitions.definition: Big frameworks or models of thinking that shape how scientists see the world and do research.
definitions.example: Before Einstein, Newton's physics was the paradigm — everyone thought that way.
definitions.first_appearance: Paragraph beginning 'We're going to walk through a graveyard'
